title: Buddham saranam gacchami
hook: a storm shelter, a friend's kitchen, a song in the car: where do you go?
tomorrow: why say the refuges three times? isn't once enough?

segments.voice: Yesterday, samma-sambuddhassa: to the one fully awake by himself, and Dhananjani's homage, worn in so deep it came out when she stumbled. The homage is done. Now the first line people say right after it.

A storm shelter is a refuge. So is the friend's kitchen you head to after a terrible day, or the song you put on in the car when the week is too loud. Nobody waits for a tornado to have one of those. You go there on ordinary days too, and that's partly why it works when things go wrong. So yesterday's question has an answer already: refuge isn't only for danger. In Pali, the line goes Buddham saranam gacchami, and the last word is the surprise.
screen: `A SHELTER, A KITCHEN, A SONG.` → `NOT ONLY FOR DANGER.` → `BUDDHAM SARANAM GACCHAMI.`

segments.voice: Word by word. Buddham: the Buddha, as the place you're headed. Saranam: refuge, shelter. Gacchami: I go. Not I believe, not I agree. I go: a verb of the feet. The chant then goes to the dhamma, his teaching, and the sangha, the community who practice it. Three refuges. The Dhammapada says that people driven by fear run to mountains, forests and sacred trees, and that this is not a safe refuge; the one who goes to the Buddha, the dhamma and the sangha comes to see the way out of suffering. So the danger it has in mind isn't a storm. It's the ordinary ache of a life that grasps. Here's a neighbor who says refuge out loud too. The Qur'an closes with a short surah that opens, in Pickthall's English, "Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind." Shared ground: both put refuge into words you say, a turning-toward spoken by heart, and that line names its Lord as Lord of all people at once, mankind. One honest difference: there, refuge is sought in God. Here, it's a teacher who woke up, his teaching and a community, and in his last days, the suttas say, the Buddha told his followers to be a refuge to themselves, with the dhamma as their refuge. Different shelters, the same human need to go somewhere. I go for refuge.
screen: `BUDDHAM, SARANAM, GACCHAMI.` · `I GO: A VERB OF THE FEET.` · `NOT MOUNTAINS, NOT SACRED TREES.` · `I SEEK REFUGE IN THE LORD OF MANKIND.` · then, large: `I GO FOR REFUGE.`

segments.voice: Count three places you already go when the week gets heavy, one on each finger: a person, a practice, a place. Thank each one quietly as you count it. Then, if you'd like, say the line once, Buddham saranam gacchami, and rest with the breath as a fourth shelter, the one you carry.
Saranam. Refuge, shelter: where you go, on bad days and good ones. Word eight of a little Pali.
Your line, said with your feet: I go for refuge. One week of Pali behind you.

howItsDone: In Theravada temples, after the homage, monks and lay people chant the three refuges in Pali: Buddham saranam gacchami, dhammam saranam gacchami, sangham saranam gacchami.

original.note: Buddham saranam gacchami in Devanagari letters: to the Buddha I go for refuge.

what a scholar hears: the Dhammapada sets the three refuges against running in fear to mountains and sacred trees, and the suttas have the Buddha tell his followers to be a refuge to themselves.

chat.says: Ava came to class. she said her neighbor prays 'I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind.' same as ours?
options: Close cousins: both say refuge aloud. That line seeks God; ours goes to the Buddha, dhamma and sangha.
Exactly the same. Every religion's refuge is really the Buddha under some other name.
Not related at all. Refuge means something completely different in every religion.
chat.meaning: Both put refuge into spoken words. In the Qur'an it is sought in God, the Lord of mankind; the Pali refuges are the Buddha, the dhamma and the sangha.

sangha.meaning: the community who practice the Buddha's teaching

notes: Unity thread (Islam): Qur'an 114:1 quoted from Pickthall 1930, 'Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind,'. Confirm exact wording and punctuation. 'The Qur'an closes with a short surah' refers to surah 114 being the last in the Qur'an's order. The difference line (refuge in God vs refuge in a teacher, teaching and community; DN 16 'be a refuge to yourselves') should be read by both a Muslim and a Theravada reader for fairness; nothing is ranked, and the script avoids 'the same'.
'that line names its Lord as Lord of all people at once, mankind' is the narrator's reading of 'Lord of mankind' (rabb an-nas) for the unity thread; a Muslim reader should confirm it is fair.
Dhp 188–192 paraphrased (Max Müller's wording not quoted). The script says the refuge leads to 'seeing the way out of suffering', compressing 190–192 (the four noble truths). Confirm.

DN 16 (Rhys Davids SBE XI, II.33 in his numbering; II.26 in PTS) paraphrased: 'be a refuge to yourselves... the dhamma as your refuge'. 'in his last days, the suttas say' hedges the timing. Confirm the section reference.
Word-by-word gloss (Buddham accusative, 'as the place you're headed') simplified for beginners; confirm.
